text: FASHION, n. A despot whom the wise ridicule and obey.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: FOLLY, n. That "gift and faculty divine" whose creative and controlling energy inspires Man's mind, guides his actions and adorns his life.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: FREEDOM, n. Exemption from the stress of authority in a beggarly half dozen of restraint's infinite multitude of methods. A political condition that every nation supposes itself to enjoy in virtual monopoly. Liberty. The distinction between freedom and liberty is not accurately known; naturalists have never been able to find a living specimen of either.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Word Book (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911)

text: The only freedom which deserves the name, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it.
locator: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859); republished in David Spitz, ed. (1975), chapter 1, p. 14

text: There is a limit to the legitimate interference of collective opinion with individual independence: and to find that limit, and maintain it against encroachment, is as indispensable to a good condition of human affairs, as protection against political despotism.
locator: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859); republished in David Spitz, ed. (1975), chapter 1, p. 6

text: Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free.
locator: Henry David Thoreau, "Walking," Excursions, p. 266 (1894). The essay on walking was first published after Thoreau's death, in Atlantic Monthly, June 1862

text: BEFRIEND, v.t. To make an ingrate.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Word Book (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: FUTURE, n. That period of time in which our affairs prosper, our friends are true and our happiness is assured.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Word Book (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: GOOD, adj. Sensible, madam, to the worth of this present writer. Alive, sir, to the advantages of letting him alone.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Word Book (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: MAGNIFICENT, adj. Having a grandeur or splendor superior to that to which the spectator is accustomed, as the ears of an ass, to a rabbit, or the glory of a glowworm, to a maggot.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: HABIT, n. A shackle for the free.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: HAPPINESS, n. An agreeable sensation arising from contemplating the misery of another.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: HATRED, n. A sentiment appropriate to the occasion of another's superiority.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: HOPE, n. Desire and expectation rolled into one.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: MEEKNESS, n. Uncommon patience in planning a revenge that is worth while.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: JESTER, n. An officer formerly attached to a king's household, whose business it was to amuse the court by ludicrous actions and utterances, the absurdity being attested by his motley costume. The king himself being attired with dignity, it took the world some centuries to discover that his own conduct and decrees were sufficiently ridiculous for the amusement not only of his court but of all mankind. The jester was commonly called a fool, but the poets and romancers have ever delighted to represent him as a singularly wise and witty person. In the circus of to-day the melancholy ghost of the court fool effects the dejection of humbler audiences with the same jests wherewith in life he gloomed the marble hall, panged the patrician sense of humor and tapped the tank of royal tears.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: IMAGINATION, n. A warehouse of facts, with poet and liar in joint ownership.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: INJURY, n. An offense next in degree of enormity to a slight.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: INVENTOR, n. A person who makes an ingenious arrangement of wheels, levers and springs, and believes it civilization.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: JEALOUS, adj. Unduly concerned about the preservation of that which can be lost only if not worth keeping.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911)

text: REPORTER, n. A writer who guesses his way to the truth and dispels it with a tempest of words.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: It was a fatal day when the public discovered that the pen is mightier than the paving-stone, and can be made as offensive as the brickbat. They at once sought for the journalist, found him, developed him, and made him their industrious and well-paid servant. It is greatly to be regretted, for both their sakes. Behind the barricade there may be much that is noble and heroic. But what is there behind the leading-article but prejudice, stupidity, cant, and twaddle? And when these four are joined together they make a terrible force, and constitute the new authority.
locator: Oscar Wilde, The Soul of Man under Socialism (1891), Wilde, Oscar, (1891 / 1912) The Soul of Man Under Socialism, London, Arthur L. Humphreys.  Retrieved from University of California Libraries Archive.org 13 February 2018  https://archive.org/details/soulofmanunderso00wildiala

text: KINDNESS, n. A brief preface to ten volumes of exaction.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Word Book (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: KISS, n. A word invented by the poets as a rhyme for "bliss." It is supposed to signify, in a general way, some kind of rite or ceremony appertaining to a good understanding; but the manner of its performance is unknown to this lexicographer.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: LANGUAGE, n. The music with which we charm the serpents guarding another's treasure.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Word Book (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: LEARNING, n. The kind of ignorance distinguishing the studious.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: LIBERTY, n. One of Imagination's most precious possessions.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: LIFE, n. A spiritual pickle preserving the body from decay. We live in daily apprehension of its loss; yet when lost it is not missed. The question, "Is life worth living?" has been much discussed; particularly by those who think it is not, many of whom have written at great length in support of their view and by careful observance of the laws of health enjoyed for long terms of years the honors of successful controversy.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: London is the epitome of our times, and the Rome of to-day.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, English Traits, Result.

text: Shallow men believe in luck, believe in circumstances: It was somebody's name, or he happened to be there at the time, or, it was so then, and another day it would have been otherwise. Strong men believe in cause and effect.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, The Conduct of Life (1860); this has also been paraphrased as "Shallow men believe in luck, believe in circumstances. Real men believe in cause and effect".

text: FIB, n. A lie that has not cut its teeth. An habitual liar's nearest approach to truth: the perigee of his eccentric orbit.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: LIAR, n. A lawyer with a roving commission.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Fine manners need the support of fine manners in others.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, The Conduct of Life, Behavior.

text: A great mind is a good sailor, as a great heart is.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, English Traits, Voyage to England, Chapter II.

text: PERSEVERANCE, n. A lowly virtue whereby mediocrity achieves an inglorious success.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: SELFISH, adj. Devoid of consideration for the selfishness of others.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Selfishness is not living as one wishes to live, it is asking others to live as one wishes to live.
locator: Oscar Wilde, The Soul of Man Under Socialism (1895)

text: Other people are quite dreadful. The only possible society is oneself.
locator: Oscar Wilde, An Ideal Husband, Act III. Reported in Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations (1922), p. 724–25.

text: There is always safety in valor.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, English Traits, The Times.

text: WEAKNESSES, n.pl. Certain primal powers of Tyrant Woman wherewith she holds dominion over the male of her species, binding him to the service of her will and paralyzing his rebellious energies.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: LABOR, n. One of the processes by which A acquires property for B.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Word Book (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: The mark of the man of the world is absence of pretension. He does not make a speech; he takes a low business-tone, avoids all brag, is nobody, dresses plainly, promises not at all, performs much, speaks in monosyllables, hugs his fact. He calls his employment by its lowest name, and so takes from evil tongues their sharpest weapon.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, The Conduct of Life (1860).

text: POLITICS, n. A strife of interests masquerading as a contest of principles.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary.

text: PRESIDENCY, n. The greased pig in the field game of American politics.
locator: Ambrose Bierce in The Devil's Dictionary.

text: PUSH, n. One of the two things mainly conducive to success, especially in politics. The other is Pull.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary, p. 270 (1948). Originally published in 1906 as The Cynic's Word Book.

text: REFLECTION, n. An action of the mind whereby we obtain a clearer view of our relation to the things of yesterday and are able to avoid the perils that we shall not again encounter.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Nature, even when she is scant and thin outwardly, satisfies us still by the assurance of a certain generosity at the roots.
locator: Henry David Thoreau, A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849).

text: CURSE, v.t. Energetically to belabor with a verbal slap-stick. This is an operation which in literature, particularly in the drama, is commonly fatal to the victim. Nevertheless, the liability to a cursing is a risk that cuts but a small figure in fixing the rates of life insurance.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: MOUSE, n. An animal which strews its path with fainting women.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: PAIN, n. An uncomfortable frame of mind that may have a physical basis in something that is being done to the body, or may be purely mental, caused by the good fortune of another.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Passion, though a bad regulator, is a powerful spring.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Considerations by the Way," The Conduct of Life (1860).

text: RECONCILIATION, n. A suspension of hostilities. An armed truce for the purpose of digging up the dead.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: READING, n. The general body of what one reads. In our country it consists, as a rule, of Indiana novels, short stories in "dialect" and humor in slang.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: RATIONAL, adj. Devoid of all delusions save those of observation, experience and reflection.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: REASON, n. Propensitate of prejudice.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: Nature will always maintain her rights, and prevail in the end over any abstract reasoning whatsoever.
locator: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) Ch.V, Part I.

text: No conclusions can be more agreeable to scepticism than such as make discoveries concerning the weakness and narrow limits of human reason and capacity.
locator: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) Ch.VII, Part II.

text: Nature must have provided some other principle, of more ready, and more general use and application; nor can an operation of such immense consequence in life, as that of inferring effects from causes, be trusted to the uncertain process of reasoning and argumentation.
locator: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) Ch.IX.

text: REBEL, n. A proponent of a new misrule who has failed to establish it.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: The stars awaken a certain reverence, because though always present, they are inaccessible; but all natural objects make a kindred impression, when the mind is open to their influence. Nature never wears a mean appearance.
locator: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Nature (1836) Ch. 1, Nature.

text: HURRICANE, n. An atmospheric demonstration once very common but now generally abandoned for the tornado and cyclone. The hurricane is still in popular use in the West Indies and is preferred by certain old-fashioned sea-captains. It is also used in the construction of the upper decks of steamboats, but generally speaking, the hurricane's usefulness has outlasted it.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Cynic's Dictionary (1906); republished as The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: I can resist everything except temptation.
locator: Oscar Wilde , Lady Windermere's Fan  (1892), Act I

text: YOUTH, n. The Period of Possibility, when Archimedes finds a fulcrum, Cassandra has a following and seven cities compete for the honor of endowing a living Homer.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).

text: ZEAL, n. A certain nervous disorder afflicting the young and inexperienced.  A passion that goeth before a sprawl.
locator: Ambrose Bierce, The Devil's Dictionary (1911).
